overview: The Sokoto Caliphate grew from the Islamic reform movement and warfare begun by Usman dan Fodio in 1804. The atlas labels its earlier Nigerian phase “Fulani Empire” and its later phase “Sokoto Caliphate”; these are connected parts of one political history, not two unrelated civilizations. Scholarship, textile production and an economy relying heavily on enslaved labor all shaped its society.

periods.title: Reform, warfare and consolidation
periods.summary: Usman dan Fodio’s movement and the developing caliphate transformed politics across much of Hausaland.

periods.title: Emirates, learning and production
periods.summary: Religious teaching and trade expanded alongside coerced agricultural labor. Experiences differed sharply by gender, status and place.

periods.title: After the loss of sovereignty
periods.summary: Colonial conquest ended the independent caliphate; later map coverage must not imply that its sovereignty continued unchanged.

sections.title: Lessons that traveled to the students

items.text: Nana Asma’u, 1793 to 1864, wrote, taught and managed a large household. Mack and Boyd describe her work in Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa and Tamachek. She belonged to a family of scholars, but her teaching reached beyond that family.

Asma’u trained traveling women teachers called jajis. They took verse lessons to women in other communities, including learners taught at home. A lesson could travel with its teacher instead of requiring everyone to reach one school building.

Recitation and memorization helped lessons spread to relatives and neighbors. Written poetry and oral teaching worked together; listening to a poem could make someone a participant even without owning a manuscript.

The surviving Admonition poem is in Hausa Ajami, with vowel marks helping readers sound out the text. Boston University dates its composition between 1855 and 1857. The reproduced copy is an undated printed witness, not a sheet known to be in Asma’u’s hand.

Asma’u’s elegies remember women’s practical care. Zaharatu assisted at births; Aisha helped orphans and widows. Such named work shows that community history included caregiving, not only the careers of male rulers.

Admonition treats obtaining food and seeking education as legitimate reasons for women to leave home. It also asks wives to follow lawful marital obligations. This was a religious argument made within her society, not a claim that its rules matched modern equality.

The poem tells believers to observe ritual washing, while allowing dry ablution during illness. The editors explain that earth or sand could be used when water was unavailable or a person was sick. This concerns religious practice; it does not establish a citywide plumbing system.

It also encourages charity and extra help for people in need. Alongside prayer and study, generosity belonged in the moral life Asma’u was teaching. Her verses are evidence of ideals being urged, not proof everyone always lived up to them.

Plantations around Sokoto, Kano, Zaria and other towns supplied food and raw materials. Salau lists millet, sorghum, cotton and indigo among the goods tied to this economy. Everyday eating and dressing depended on large amounts of agricultural work.

That work often came from enslaved people. Salau distinguishes supervised labor gangs, work alongside owners and arrangements requiring payments to owners. Different arrangements did not remove the fundamental denial of freedom.

Muhammad Bello promoted agricultural settlement as part of consolidating the state. Lovejoy connects these policies with textile production in southern Kano and northern Zaria: fields, spinning, weaving, dyeing and trade belonged to an interconnected economy.

No single plantation export crop dominated the whole caliphate. Food markets and textile making were both important. This helps explain why a history of the state must include workshops and farms, not just armies.

sections.title: A written greeting and a political ending

items.text: “بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم” means “In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.” This Arabic invocation opens the scanned printed witness of Admonition, before its Hausa Ajami verses. Here it is shown without vowel marks. The surviving printed copy is not known to be in Asma’u’s own hand.

British forces took Kano and Sokoto in 1903 amid the wider European partition of the caliphate’s territories. Loss of independent government did not end Muslim scholarship or the communities whose lives had made the state.

Asma’u’s educational work remained influential long after her lifetime. SOAS’s account of her writings and Jean Boyd’s scholarship documents a continuing legacy of women teaching women, rather than a tradition that simply stopped when the state was conquered.

ending.text: Colonial conquest ended the independent Sokoto Caliphate in 1903. Its territories were divided under European rule, while Muslim communities and traditions of scholarship continued. The later 1914 map endpoint is not the end date of independent Sokoto.
